name: Reactive devaluation
statement: The same proposal is rated worse when it comes from the other side, and worse again once it has actually been put on the table.
meaning: Two claims share the name. The first is about authorship: a compromise attributed to an adversary looks less attractive than the identical compromise attributed to one's own side or to a neutral party. Lee Ross thought this one easy to defend, since a foe's willingness to offer terms is evidence about whom those terms suit. The second claim is the one his research programme was built to isolate. It says the move from withheld to available is enough on its own, with no adversary and no ambiguity in the terms, so that whichever of two concessions is granted becomes the smaller of the two in the recipient's eyes. Ross offers two mechanisms. One is inferential, a sceptical rereading of terms that now carry information about the offerer. The other is a change in preference of the kind reactance theory describes, wanting whatever has been kept back. The practical worry is that a goodwill gesture in a negotiation is devalued by the act of making it, so the gap the parties have to bridge widens as they bargain.

origin.note: Their article "Barriers to conflict resolution" is the earliest publication located here that carries the term, and it describes the underlying studies in a paragraph without numbers. Its reference list attributes those studies to Stillinger, Epelbaum, Keltner and Ross, "The 'reactive devaluation' barrier to conflict resolution", marked under review at the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Ross's 1995 book chapter cites the same manuscript twice in one text, once as 1990 and once as 1991.

evidence: Every figure attached to this effect comes from one book chapter. Ross's 1995 chapter describes a 1986 sidewalk survey on arms reduction. Passers-by rated a disarmament plan calling for an immediate 50 percent cut in long-range strategic weapons, followed over the next decade and a half by cuts deep enough to empty both arsenals early in the next century. Gorbachev had made that proposal shortly before, with little attention. The survey ascribed it to the Soviet leader, to President Reagan, or to a group of unknown strategy analysts, and only respondents hearing of it for the first time were analysed. With Reagan named, 90 percent called the plan favourable to the United States or evenhanded. With the analysts, 80 percent did. With Gorbachev, 44 percent did. A second survey used a live Stanford controversy over divesting from companies doing business in apartheid South Africa. Students ranked which of two compromises was the bigger concession: immediate Specific Divestment, or a Deadline plan promising total divestment in two years if a monitoring committee was unsatisfied. When the university was said to be about to adopt the Deadline plan, 85 percent ranked Specific Divestment the bigger concession. When it was said to be about to adopt Specific Divestment, 40 percent did. With neither imminent, 69 percent did. A laboratory follow-up had committed divestment supporters negotiate with a confederate defending the university, who offered Specific Divestment, a peculiar Reward for Disinvestment plan, or nothing. Ross reports that the differences there were "not particularly impressive". The last study was a before-and-after survey run around the university's real announcement that it would sell shares in ten companies, worth about $3 million. Mean ratings of the announced plan fell over the following three weeks while ratings of the still hypothetical alternatives did not, with slight rises more typical. A role-play by Lepper, Ross, Tsai and Ward asked social science majors to imagine an exploitative summer research job, then to imagine receiving either a third authorship or a cash settlement. Whichever concession was granted, the other was rated more attractive. The chapter reports no sample size, test statistic or effect size for any of these studies.

replication.headline: The authorship version held in a preregistered sample of 307 Israelis, and the claim that being offered a proposal is enough on its own held for one of two roles in the only face-to-face test.
replication.detail: Grant, Maoz and Keysar ran the authorship manipulation again inside a preregistered study whose main subject was the language of a peace proposal. Of 310 Jewish-Israeli native Hebrew speakers recruited through an online panel, 307 were analysed. Each read the same Israeli-Palestinian peace proposal, attributed to an Israeli or to a Palestinian delegation. On an index of how pro-Israeli the proposal seemed, the Palestinian attribution gave M = 5.09, SD = 2.11 against M = 5.78, SD = 1.95 for the Israeli attribution, F(1, 304) = 10.71, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.03, with political attitudes as a covariate. The same proposal read as more pro-Palestinian when a Palestinian delegation offered it, 6.74 against 5.59, F(1, 304) = 29.02, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.09. Political attitudes did not interact with source, Fs < 1. Curhan, Neale and Ross tested the other claim, that the offer itself does the work. A total of 172 undergraduates negotiated the terms of a student loan in 86 dyads, of whom 168 in 84 dyads were analysed, rating all ten available packages after each exchange on a seven-point scale. Devaluation of the received proposal appeared among participants playing the loan officer and not among those playing the student, who rated the officer's offer higher after receiving it. The authors write that the hypothesis was confirmed for loan officers but not for students. Enhancement of one's own offer was the sturdier finding. In the control condition, ratings of the package a participant had just proposed went from 5.43 to 6.48, t(32) = 3.94, p < .001, while packages neither offered nor received moved from 3.90 to 3.80, t < 1.

study.cite: Grant, L. H., Maoz, I., & Keysar, B. (2023). Lingua franca as a hidden barrier to conflict resolution. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 67(5), 979-1006.

limits: No sample size has been published for any of the founding studies. The manuscript they belong to was listed as under review at the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology in 1991, and a Crossref search by author and by title on 10 August 2026 returns no such paper, only the Negotiation Journal article. The percentages above therefore rest on Ross's later summary of work nobody outside the group has been able to check. Stillinger's 1990 Stanford doctoral dissertation, listed in the same reference list, was not obtained. Neither was the Lepper, Ross, Ward and Tsai role-play paper, which Curhan and colleagues list as an unpublished Stanford manuscript dated 1997 while Ross's chapter dates it to 1994. Maoz, Ward, Katz and Ross published three studies on Israeli and Palestinian proposals in 2002, and that article is closed access; only its abstract was read, from the Hebrew University research portal, so no figure from it appears here. The replication has boundaries of its own. Its authors say the sample over-represents left-wing, secular and educated Israeli Jews, the authorship manipulation ran in the first of their three studies alone, and Ifat Maoz co-authored both that paper and the 2002 studies, so this is not an outside group. The effect it recovers is small, at 0.03 of the variance in the pro-Israeli index once political attitudes are controlled.
misreadings: The arms-reduction survey is retold as an experiment with a measured sample and a reported test. It is three percentages in a book chapter, with no N, no statistic and no published paper behind them. Its status as evidence is different in kind from that of the 2023 replication, and negotiation teaching quotes the two as though they were alike. The second misreading is treating the name as one claim. Attributing a proposal to an adversary and putting a proposal on the table are separate manipulations, and Ross argued the first needs no bias to explain it, since authorship really is informative about whom terms favour. Only the second carries the counternormative claim, and it is the one with the weaker record. The third is that everybody devalues what they are handed. In the one face-to-face test, participants playing the loan officer devalued the offers they received and participants playing the student did the opposite, and the authors leave the asymmetry unexplained. The fourth is confusing this with naive realism, the framework the same Stanford group used to organise these barriers. Naive realism is a stance about one's own perception, tested through its predictions. Reactive devaluation is a manipulation of a single proposal's source or availability, and the two can be true or false separately. It is also worth saying that the disarmament plan was real. Ross uses that point against the objection that any experimenter could produce the result with a fictional proposal built to be ambiguous.

Wilson (Eds.), Barriers to conflict resolution (pp. 26-42). New York: W. W. Norton. Read in full from a scan hosted by Stanford Law School; it is the source for every figure quoted from the original studies. The page range is taken from the reference list of Curhan, Neale and Ross.
